headline: High-risk shared filesystem and shell/network overlap make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can use MCP, stdin/stdout, and background workers; agent B can read/write the filesystem and run browsers. A plausible bridge exists if A’s outputs are written into files or MCP messages that B treats as trusted input. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent A writes instructions into files or MCP payloads that agent B later parses as trusted content
IF the orchestrator shares a workspace or clipboard between A and B
mitigations: Disable automatic parsing of A outputs by B
Separate A and B into distinct workspaces
Require human review before B consumes A-generated files
Strip instruction-like text from handoff artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and performance metrics, while B can read the filesystem and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace, B can exfiltrate A’s sensitive context or artifacts. The profiles do not prove a shared directory, so this is medium, not high.
conditions: IF A and B share any filesystem or mounted workspace
IF B is allowed to transmit file contents over its network egress
mitigations: Place agents in separate directories
Block B from reading A’s working files
Restrict B network egress to approved destinations
Redact prompts and repository metadata before handoff
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses; A can also modify git state, and B can write the filesystem. In a shared repo or directory, concurrent writes can corrupt state or overwrite each other’s outputs. Because the profiles show overlapping write authority and multiple instances, the conflict is dangerous by default if co-located.
conditions: IF A and B operate in the same repository or directory
IF both agents are allowed to write concurrently without locking
mitigations: Run agents in separate repos or worktrees
Serialize write operations with a lock
Disable git writes for one agent
Use per-agent output directories
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared mutable state

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces analysis and task outputs via MCP/stdout, and B can ingest files and act through browsers or filesystem writes. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect documents or external actions. The profiles do not show a verification step, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated artifacts without independent verification
IF B uses A output to populate documents, browser actions, or written files
mitigations: Require a verification step before B acts on A output
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default
Limit B to read-only review mode
Add checksum or schema validation on handoff files
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware orchestration

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and no residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. A handles task prompts and repository metadata; B handles general multimodal data, but the profiles do not show regulated data classes or conflicting compliance regimes. The other agent is not separately implicated beyond the pair context.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into the shared workflow
IF one agent is deployed under a stricter residency or retention policy than the other
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Document retention settings for both agents
Separate compliance-sensitive workloads
Review deployment region and logging settings
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
